body_regions.description: Brain and sleep: alertness, reaction time and mood.
body_regions.name: Head

body_regions.alert: Eyesight can change on long missions. In a NASA survey of about 300 astronauts, around 60% of those on long flights reported worse near or distance vision, and for some the changes were still there years after landing. The cause is spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS): a swollen optic nerve, a flattened back of the eye and a far-sighted shift. Astronauts do not go blind, but vision can stay blurred. Run both eye tests regularly and report any change.
body_regions.description: Vision. On long missions the eye can change shape and blur near sight (spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome, SANS). Two checks are logged here, the same kinds NASA uses on the ISS: a near-vision test and an Amsler grid.
body_regions.name: Eyes

body_regions.description: The inner ear senses balance. In weightlessness it can cause space motion sickness, with dizziness, nausea and unsteadiness. A daily self-rating tracks it.
body_regions.name: Ears and balance

body_regions.description: Arm muscles and grip. Muscles that no longer carry weight lose strength without exercise. A handgrip reading tracks upper-body strength.
body_regions.name: Arms

body_regions.description: Calcium released from bone in weightlessness raises the risk of kidney stones, and drinking enough water helps. Urine colour is a quick hydration check.
body_regions.name: Kidneys

body_regions.description: Leg bones, muscles and daily activity.
body_regions.name: Legs

body_regions.description: Temperature, body mass and general readings.
body_regions.name: Whole body

indicators.how_to_measure:
Sit still for 2 minutes.
Place two fingertips on the inside of your wrist, below the thumb.
Count the beats for 15 seconds, or use Count my pulse.
Multiply the count by 4.
indicators.name: Heart rate
indicators.why_it_matters: In microgravity, fluids move toward the head and the heart works differently. Heart rate is often one of the first vitals to change with fatigue, illness or dehydration.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Rest seated for 5 minutes.
Put the cuff on your upper arm, level with your heart.
Start the monitor and keep still until it finishes.
Record the top number (systolic).
indicators.name: Systolic blood pressure
indicators.why_it_matters: Fluid shifts in microgravity change blood pressure, especially when you stand up after flight. Readings far from your usual level need a check before any strenuous activity.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Use the same measurement as the systolic reading.
Find the bottom number on the monitor.
Record the bottom number (diastolic).
indicators.name: Diastolic blood pressure
indicators.why_it_matters: Diastolic pressure shows the pressure between heartbeats. It is read together with the systolic value, not on its own.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Clip the probe on a relaxed, warm fingertip.
Keep still until the reading holds steady for 30 seconds.
Record the number shown.
indicators.name: Blood oxygen (SpO2)
indicators.why_it_matters: Cabin air is controlled, but breathing and blood oxygen can still change in flight. Low oxygen can cause dizziness, breathlessness and confusion.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Take the digital thermometer from the medical kit.
Place it as the kit instructions say and wait for the beep.
Record the reading to one decimal place.
indicators.name: Body temperature
indicators.why_it_matters: Infection and dehydration can raise temperature, and a cold cabin or long rest can lower it. Changes should be checked early, because the crew has limited medical resources.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Wash and dry your hands.
Prick the side of a fingertip with the lancet.
Apply a drop of blood to the test strip and read the meter.
indicators.name: Blood glucose
indicators.why_it_matters: Stress, poor sleep and changes in eating during flight can shift blood sugar. Very high or very low readings need prompt action. In the Inspiration4 crew (4 people, 3-day flight), lab glucose averaged 75 mg/dL before launch and 93 mg/dL the day after landing.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Think back over the last 24 hours.
Add up all the time you slept, including naps.
Round to the nearest half hour and record it.
indicators.name: Sleep last night
indicators.why_it_matters: Light and work schedules in orbit and in transit shift sleep. Poor sleep reduces alertness, slows reactions and lowers mood.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Look at the five faces, from very low to very good.
Pick the one that best matches how you feel right now.
There is no wrong answer.
indicators.name: Mood
indicators.why_it_matters: Confinement, isolation and distance from family can lower mood. Low mood often comes before problems with sleep and performance.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Start the reaction test on the tablet.
Tap the target as soon as it changes colour.
The test runs five times and keeps the median.
indicators.name: Reaction time
indicators.why_it_matters: Radiation and sleep loss can affect the brain and reaction speed. Slower reactions raise the risk of mistakes in tasks that need care.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Think of today's countermeasure sessions.
Add the minutes of treadmill, cycle and resistance exercise.
Enter the total in minutes.
indicators.name: Exercise today
indicators.why_it_matters: Without loading, bone and muscle lose strength in microgravity. Daily exercise is the main countermeasure against that loss.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Measure before food or drink, after using the toilet.
Strap in the body mass device and sit still while it moves you on its spring.
Wait for the device to show your mass, then record it to 0.1 kg.
indicators.name: Body mass
indicators.why_it_matters: Body mass can fall in flight when appetite or food intake drops. Watch the trend over several days, not single readings.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Think about your back pain today.
Compare it with the scale: none, mild, moderate, severe or very severe.
Pick the label that fits and note where the pain is in the notes field.
indicators.name: Back pain
indicators.why_it_matters: The spine lengthens in microgravity and back muscles unload. Back pain can disturb sleep and work, and severe or new pain needs a check.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Open the food log for today.
Add up the calories printed on each package you ate.
Include drinks with calories and snacks.
Enter the total in kcal.
indicators.name: Food eaten today
indicators.why_it_matters: In flight, food can taste blander and appetite often drops, so crew can eat less than they burn. Low intake leads to weight loss and muscle and bone loss. Your lower limit is calculated from your sex, age, height and pre-flight mass using the NASA-STD-3001 EER standard (activity factor 1.25, rounded to 10 kcal).

indicators.how_to_measure:
Count the drink pouches and cups you finished today.
Use the volume printed on each pouch.
Include water, tea, coffee and juice, not food.
Enter the total in mL.
indicators.name: Fluids drunk today
indicators.why_it_matters: Thirst is weaker in microgravity and fluid moves toward the head, so crew often drink less than they need. Too little fluid raises heart rate and the risk of kidney stones. The lower limit is the NASA minimum of 2000 mL drinking water a day.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Check for a sore throat, cough, blocked nose or fever feeling.
Check your skin for rash or cold sores.
Compare all of this with the scale: none, mild, moderate, marked or severe.
Pick the label that fits and list the symptoms in the notes.
indicators.name: Illness symptoms
indicators.why_it_matters: Spaceflight stress and a closed cabin change how the immune system works. Old viruses such as cold sores can wake up, and rashes can appear. A small illness spreads fast in a small crew, so report it early.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Think about the last 24 hours.
Ask how tense, worried or overloaded you felt.
Pick the label on the scale that fits best.
There is no wrong answer.
indicators.name: Stress
indicators.why_it_matters: Months in a small, sealed space with high workload and no way out raise stress. Long stress harms sleep, mood and judgement. It often shows before other problems.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Think about the last 24 hours.
Ask how close you felt to your crew and to people at home.
Pick the label on the scale that fits best.
There is no wrong answer.
indicators.name: Social connection
indicators.why_it_matters: Isolation, confinement and distance from family can leave crew feeling alone, even in a full crew. Feeling cut off often comes before low mood and conflict. Talking early helps.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Set up once: hold a bank card to the screen and match the on-screen rectangle to it.
Hold the screen 40 cm from your eyes with both eyes open and your reading glasses on.
For each letter E, tap the direction it points: the side where the three bars end.
The letters get smaller each line. The test stops when you get fewer than 3 of 5 right.
The result is the smallest line you passed. Lower is better; 0.0 is sharp.
indicators.name: Near vision (eye chart)
indicators.why_it_matters: SANS is the main eye risk of long missions. In a NASA study of about 300 astronauts, around 60% on long flights and 29% on short flights reported worse near or distance vision, and some changes were still there years after landing (Mader et al. 2011). The usual complaint is blurred near vision from a far-sighted shift, so near vision is what is tested. This test is a screening estimate to track change from your own baseline, and the ranges here are assumptions.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Set up once: match a bank card to the rectangle on the screen.
Hold the screen about 28 cm from one eye and cover the other eye with your palm.
Look only at the centre dot.
Tap every square that looks wavy, blurred, dark or missing.
Repeat with the other eye. The result is the total squares marked for both eyes.
indicators.name: Amsler grid (distorted squares)
indicators.why_it_matters: NASA has the Amsler grid on the ISS to check the centre of vision. Long missions can cause SANS: a swollen optic nerve, a flattened back of the eye and choroidal folds. About 15% of astronauts had clinically significant optic disc swelling after long flights, and choroidal folds were seen in over 20% (Lee et al. 2020). Any distortion needs a report to the flight surgeon. The 0 and 5 limits here are assumptions.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Think about the last 24 hours.
Note any dizziness, nausea, spinning or unsteadiness, especially when you move your head.
Pick the label that fits your worst moment.
Note what set it off in the notes field.
indicators.name: Balance and dizziness
indicators.why_it_matters: The inner ear senses gravity. In weightlessness it gets mixed signals, which can cause space motion sickness (dizziness, nausea, unsteadiness), mostly in the first days. Balance can also feel unsteady for a few days after landing. Dizziness that stays or is severe needs a check.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Look at your urine in a clear container or the bowl, in good light.
Compare it with a urine colour chart, from 1 (very pale) to 8 (brown).
Pick the number that is closest.
If you cannot see it well, skip this check.
indicators.name: Urine colour
indicators.why_it_matters: Weightlessness releases calcium from bone, which raises the risk of kidney stones, and drinking too little makes stones more likely. Darker urine is a quick sign of low fluid intake. The limits follow published urine colour charts, not NASA limits. Blood in the urine or pain in the side needs medical advice now.

indicators.how_to_measure:
Use a handgrip dynamometer (a hand squeeze gauge).
Sit or stand with your arm at your side and the elbow bent a little.
Squeeze as hard as you can for 3 seconds.
Do it twice with your stronger hand and type the better value.
indicators.name: Grip strength
indicators.why_it_matters: Muscles that carry no weight lose strength in microgravity unless the crew exercise. Grip strength is a simple check of arm strength. Compare it with your own pre-flight value: a steady fall means the exercise plan needs a look. Your watch limit uses the EWGSOP2 low-strength cut-off by sex (27 kg for men, 16 kg for women). These are cut-offs by sex, not severity levels, so the app has no alert limit for grip.

missions.description: Low Earth orbit, about 420 km up (approximate). Earth's magnetic field blocks most solar particles, so the solar particle factor is low. Mission control leads medical decisions and replies within seconds.
missions.name: International Space Station

missions.description: Crew capsule in cislunar space between Earth and the Moon, roughly 250,000 km from Earth on average (approximate; it changes along the trajectory). Zero gravity, a small cabin and thin shielding outside Earth's magnetic field. The storm shelter is a corner of the cabin walled with crew stowage bags (assumption). Medical decisions are shared between the crew and mission control with a signal delay of about 1 second one way (approximate).
missions.name: Lunar transit spacecraft

missions.description: Surface base about 384,400 km from Earth (approximate). The base structure gives some shielding, but there is no magnetic field shield. Medical decisions are shared between the crew and mission control.
missions.name: Lunar surface base

missions.description: Crew in a pressurized rover on a multi-day traverse, about 50 km from the lunar base (approximate), so roughly 384,450 km from Earth. Lunar gravity (0.166 g, same as the surface base) and thin hull shielding. Return to the base takes hours to a day or two; the evacuation time shown is to Earth care (approximate). The crew leads medical decisions and consults mission control when needed (signal delay about 1.3 seconds one way).
missions.name: Pressurized lunar rover

missions.description: Transit toward Mars. Average distance about 225 million km (approximate; it changes with orbital position). One-way signal delay can reach about 22 minutes. The crew leads medical decisions. Gravity is set to 0 for transit (assumption).
missions.name: Mars mission

The app's exponential factor is set to match that (exp(-20/70) = 0.75); above 20 g/cm2 it slightly overstates the benefit.

sources.note: Stay active and try exercises and stretches for back pain. The crew handbook posture is a prototype step.
sources.title: Back pain advice: NHS

sources.note: AHA: rest at least 5 minutes, no caffeine or exercise within 30 minutes; above 180/120 with chest pain, vision change, weakness or confusion is an emergency. NHS low blood pressure: drink water and stand up slowly (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/low-blood-pressure-hypotension/); lie down with legs raised if faint (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fainting/). Re-measure times and crew steps are prototype steps.
sources.title: Blood pressure advice: AHA and NHS

sources.note: Move your head carefully and slowly (NHS vertigo); avoid sudden movements or position changes (MedlinePlus, https://medlineplus.gov/ency/patientinstructions/000692.htm). Crew steps are prototype steps.
sources.title: Dizziness advice: NHS and MedlinePlus

sources.note: Low: take 15 g of fast carbohydrate and recheck after 15 minutes (CDC). High: drink plenty of water, check ketones at 250 mg/dL or more for 2 hours; vomiting, confusion or heavy breathing need urgent care (ADA, https://diabetes.org/living-with-diabetes/managing-ketones). CDC sick-day advice: keep taking diabetes medicine as usual (https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/living-with/managing-sick-days.html). Holding food and the crew steps are prototype steps.
sources.title: Blood glucose advice: CDC and American Diabetes Association

sources.note: Grip strength is recorded as the best or mean of up to three attempts. The other steps are prototype steps.
sources.title: Grip strength test: Roberts et al. 2011, Age and Ageing

sources.note: Very high or low heart rate with chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness or fainting is an emergency (AHA; NHS SVT, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/supraventricular-tachycardia-svt/). The rest and re-measure times and the crew medical officer and ground steps are prototype steps.
sources.title: Heart rate advice: AHA and NHS

sources.note: Drinking fluids regularly reduces the risk of dehydration; dark yellow pee and dizziness are signs (NHS). Too much water can lower blood sodium: headache, confusion and nausea are signs (MedlinePlus hyponatremia, https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000394.htm). Kidney stone risk: NASA renal stone report (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170004709/downloads/20170004709.pdf). Crew steps are prototype steps.
sources.title: Fluid advice: NHS and MedlinePlus

sources.note: Short naps of 15-30 minutes increase alertness (NIOSH). Avoid caffeine in the afternoon or evening (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/index.html).
sources.title: Sleep advice: NIOSH and CDC

sources.note: Contact a provider at 92% or lower and get emergency care at 88% or lower. Sitting upright, a warm finger and the re-measure times are prototype steps.
sources.title: Blood oxygen advice: MedlinePlus

sources.note: Fever: rest and drink plenty of fluids (NHS); one layer of lightweight clothing (MedlinePlus Fever). Low temperature: wrap in a blanket and give a warm non-alcoholic drink; below 35 C is an emergency (NHS hypothermia, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hypothermia/). Re-measure times and crew steps are prototype steps.
sources.title: Temperature advice: NHS and MedlinePlus

sources.note: Measured by the Tissue-Equivalent Proportional Counter (TEPC) on the ISS, a single station instrument, so this is a station-average rate, not a per-module value. Time-weighted mean of DOSE_EQ60 over 12 two-day windows spread across 2017 (windows with no reading were skipped): 0.884 mSv/day. Used as the ISS gcr_msv_per_day. Dataset covers 2010-04-29 to 2018-04-11; run tools/fetch_tepc.py to recompute.
sources.title: ISS TEPC dose analyzer (CDAWeb HAPI)

sources.note: CDC: healthy weight is BMI 18.5 to under 25, obesity 30 or more. NASA astronaut candidates had to be 62-75 inches (157-190 cm) tall (NASA Facts, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/606877main_fs-2011-11-057-jsc-astro_trng.pdf). BMI 18.5 at 1.57 m = 46 kg and BMI 25 at 1.90 m = 90 kg give the normal band; BMI 30 at 1.90 m = 108 kg is the upper alert. WHO: BMI below 16 carries a markedly increased risk of ill health (https://apps.who.int/nutrition/landscape/help.aspx?helpid=420); BMI 16 at 1.57 m = 39 kg is the lower alert. Change from your own pre-flight mass matters more: NASA reports typical in-flight losses of 1-5% (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150000512/downloads/20150000512.pdf).
sources.title: Body mass limits: CDC BMI categories at NASA astronaut heights

sources.note: AHA: stage 1 high blood pressure starts at 130/80; above 180/120 needs prompt care. MedlinePlus: 90/60 or lower is low blood pressure (https://medlineplus.gov/lowbloodpressure.html). NEWS2: systolic 90 or lower scores 3 points, 91-100 scores 2 (https://www.rcp.ac.uk/media/alxev00t/news2-chart-1_the-news-scoring-system_0_0.pdf). No published diastolic-only low alert was found, so the app has none.
sources.title: Blood pressure limits: AHA, MedlinePlus and NEWS2

sources.note: At least 2000 mL of drinking water per crew member per day (section 6.3.2.1). The US National Academies set no upper limit for water (https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/10925/chapter/6), so the app has none. NASA's renal stone report says stone risk rises when urine volume drops below 1.5 L/day (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170004709/downloads/20170004709.pdf).
sources.title: Fluid intake: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev B, V2 6029

sources.note: CDC: below 70 mg/dL is low, below 54 mg/dL is severe. Two hours after a glucose drink, 140 mg/dL or below is normal (https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/diabetes-testing/index.html). ADA: check ketones when blood glucose is 250 mg/dL or more for 2 hours (https://diabetes.org/living-with-diabetes/managing-ketones).
sources.title: Blood glucose limits: CDC and American Diabetes Association

sources.note: EWGSOP2 low grip strength cut-offs: below 27 kg for men and below 16 kg for women. These are cut-offs by sex, not severity levels. The app applies each astronaut's sex-specific cut-off as the watch limit (falling back to 16 kg if sex is unknown) and has no alert limit.
sources.title: Grip strength: EWGSOP2 (Cruz-Jentoft et al. 2019)

sources.note: Normal resting heart rate 60-100 bpm (AHA, All About Heart Rate). Watch below 50 and alert below 40 or above 130 follow the Royal College of Physicians NEWS2 chart: 41-50 bpm scores 1 point, 40 or lower and 131 or higher score 3 points (https://www.rcp.ac.uk/media/alxev00t/news2-chart-1_the-news-scoring-system_0_0.pdf).
sources.title: Heart rate limits: American Heart Association and NEWS2

sources.note: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev B, V2 7003, Table 11 (activity factor 1.25): men EER = 622 - 9.53 x age + 1.25 x (15.9 x kg + 539.6 x m); women EER = 354 - 6.91 x age + 1.25 x (9.36 x kg + 726 x m), rounded to the nearest 10 kcal using pre-flight mass. When sex, birth year, height or pre-flight mass is missing, the app falls back to 2300 kcal/day. No upper limit is set. Measured ISS intake was about 2300-2450 kcal/day (NASA nutrition evidence report, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150000512/downloads/20150000512.pdf).
sources.title: Energy needs: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev B, V2 7003

sources.note: Psychomotor vigilance test: alert people typically average 200-300 ms (Basner et al. 2020). Responses of 500 ms or more are lapses and responses under 100 ms are false starts (Basner & Dinges 2011, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3079937). Tablet touch latency can add time, so compare with your own baseline.
sources.title: Reaction time limits: Basner et al. 2020 and Basner & Dinges 2011

sources.note: MedlinePlus: normal saturation 95-100%; contact a provider at 92% or lower, emergency care at 88% or lower. NEWS2: an oxygen saturation of 91% or lower scores 3 points (https://www.rcp.ac.uk/media/alxev00t/news2-chart-1_the-news-scoring-system_0_0.pdf), so the alert is below 92.
sources.title: Blood oxygen limits: MedlinePlus and NEWS2

sources.note: Normal 36.1-37.2 C (MedlinePlus Body temperature norms). An adult probably has a fever above 37.2-37.5 C, and over 38 C most often means a fever (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003090.htm). Hypothermia is below 35 C (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000038.htm).
sources.title: Body temperature limits: MedlinePlus

sources.note: On the 8-colour chart, keep urine below shade four (USADA, https://www.usada.org/spirit-of-sport/hydration-101-need-know/), so watch above 3. Published cut-offs for dehydration range from 3 or below to 5 or below (Wardenaar et al. 2021), so alert above 5.
sources.title: Urine colour: USADA and Wardenaar et al. 2021

sources.note: ISS crew exercise about 2 hours a day (see also CSA, https://asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/astronauts/living-exercising.asp). The app gives full exercise credit at 120 min/day.

Used: visual acuity and Amsler grid are available on the ISS; about 15% of astronauts had clinically significant optic disc edema after long flights; choroidal folds in over 20%; all affected astronauts were correctable to 20/20 but some had residual refractive changes for several years; decreased near vision (hyperopic shift) was the main symptom. sources.note: Abstract (read via Europe PMC, PMID 21849212): 7 astronauts after about 6 months on the ISS, 6 with decreased near vision; postflight questionnaires of about 300 astronauts: about 29% (short flights) and 60% (long flights) had worse distant and near vision; some changes unresolved years after flight. The app's ranges are not taken from it.
sources.title: Mader et al. 2011, Ophthalmology: Optic disc edema, globe flattening, choroidal folds, and hyperopic shifts observed in astronauts after long-duration space flight

sources.note: NASA JSC grades: mild (no operational impact), moderate (minimal impact) and severe (significant performance decrement, may last beyond 72 hours). The app treats Mild as normal and alerts at Severe or worse. NASA's grades are given by a flight surgeon; the self-rating here is our adaptation.
sources.title: NASA space motion sickness grading (Davis et al. 1988)

sources.note: An August 1972 class event gives a dose rate of about 50 mSv/h behind 5 g/cm2 aluminium (model). The October 1989 events lasted about three days, so an event with no end time is given 72 hours (NOAA SWPC: radiation storms last hours to days, https://www.spaceweather.gov/phenomena/solar-radiation-storm).
sources.title: Wilson et al.: Biological response to SPE exposures (NASA)

sources.note: RAD measured about 1.8 mSv/day dose equivalent inside the spacecraft during the cruise to Mars.
sources.title: Zeitlin et al. 2013, Science: radiation during the Mars Science Laboratory cruise

sources.note: Chang'e-4 LND measured 1369 microSv/day dose equivalent on the lunar surface behind about 3.5 mm aluminium, used as 1.37 mSv/day for the surface base. The rover uses the same value (assumption: similar thin shielding).
sources.title: Zhang et al. 2020, Science Advances: first measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface
